name: Tomas Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead operator on the filling line at a soft drinks bottling plant, out past the retail park. We do fizzy drinks and some juice in plastic bottles. The line goes blow-moulder, filler, capper, labeller, shrink-wrap, and at full speed it's about four hundred bottles a minute. My job is to keep that number up. Changeovers between flavours, cleaning cycles, fixing the labeller when it starts putting labels on crooked.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the numbers, honestly. I keep a little notebook, every shift, bottles per minute, downtime, why. When we beat our record, I bring in pastries. What wears me out is rotating shifts, mornings one week, lates the next, and the pay, which is a bit lower than the brewery in the city. But the brewery's an hour away and Nadia works at the dentist's here in town, so we stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, so it was a useful tool and nothing more. I use it now and then to tidy up my shift reports, and that saves me ten minutes. I'd tell the guys, good, now let's get back to beating our record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. My job's safe as it ever was, which is not totally safe, but normal. I'd probably keep using the tool for reports and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Ask for the shift manager post if it opens. Maybe finally put together a proper budget with Nadia, because we keep saying we will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty normal, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not totally safe. What's normally the threat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Head office. Every couple of years they talk about moving bottling to the big site in the north and closing us. Then the transport costs come up and they change their minds. That's the real worry here, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put a budget together. What would be in it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage, the car loan, the kids' stuff. Yusuf's fifteen and eats like a horse, and Hana wants a phone. I've never written it down because I'm scared of what the bottom line says. Funny for someone who writes down every bottle.

S0.say: I'd say AI was a useful tool and nothing more; I use it to tidy shift reports and save ten minutes. Then I'd tell the crew to get back to beating our record.
S0.think: I think I'd be fine, with my job about as safe as it ever was. I'd keep using the tool for reports and leave it there.
S0.do: Carries on leading the filling line and applies for the shift manager post if it opens. Sits down with his partner to write a proper household budget for the first time.
S0.quote: I've never written it down because I'm scared of what the bottom line says. Funny for someone who writes down every bottle.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas is a numbers person at work who avoids the numbers at home, and he noticed the irony himself. His long-standing threat is head office closing the plant, not technology. He's a measured voice who doesn't dramatise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, it's coming, let's be smart about it. There's no point fighting it and no point pretending it's all great either. Work out what changes on our line and get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my line's already pretty automatic, and the next step is a system that runs changeovers and spots faults on its own. That could cut the crew. I think they'd keep a lead, but maybe one lead for two lines instead of one each.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tool more seriously, not just for reports, maybe for working out why the labeller jams. Once I saw other plants using a system that works, I'd ask to be trained on it. And I'd start saving twenty-five a week, which is what I can find without the kids noticing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. I'd feel like I can keep up if I'm careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: One lead for two lines. Who would you be up against?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mo, on line one. He's a friend, we've done twelve years side by side. I think I'm better on the numbers and he's better with the crew. I'd hate it to come down to us two, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see other plants using it first. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen two systems come in here and get ripped out. I'm not going to be the first one to bet on something. When the plant in the north has had it a year and it works, then I'm in.

S1.say: I'd say it's coming, so let's be smart about it, neither fighting it nor pretending it's all great. Work out what changes on our line and get ready.
S1.think: I think a system that runs changeovers and spots faults could cut the crew, maybe to one lead for two lines. That could put me up against my friend Mo.
S1.do: Uses the AI tool more seriously, including for diagnosing labeller jams, and asks for training once other plants have proven the new system. Saves about twenty-five a week.
S1.feel: Uneasy but okay, confident he can keep up if he's careful.
S1.quote: When the plant in the north has had it a year and it works, then I'm in.
S1.fieldNote: Tomas is a classic second mover: he's seen two systems ripped out and won't bet early. His biggest worry here is personal, not abstract: competing with his friend Mo for one lead job. Saving twenty-five a week is a small but real step for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shock and the government needs to help people through it, sensibly. Not throw money at everything, but help with mortgages and training. I'd say it at work and maybe post once, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'd be in trouble. The bottling plant would be one of the first places to go fully automatic, because it's already halfway there. Nadia's reception job probably goes too, with an AI answering the phone. I'd be lying if I said I had a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down and do that budget I've been avoiding, and cut the car loan by selling the newer car. I'd start looking straight away for anything local that robots aren't doing yet, delivery, building, maybe a job in maintenance. And I'd ask Nadia's parents if they could help with the mortgage for a few months, which would be hard for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It'd keep me up at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would asking her parents be hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when we got married her dad said, you'll look after her, yes? And I said yes. Asking him for money is like admitting I didn't. He'd help, though. He'd also mention it at every birthday for ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with Yusuf and Hana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yusuf's fifteen. I'd tell him straight, because he'd find out anyway, and I'd ask him to not ask for anything for a while. Hana's eleven. I'd tell her the phone has to wait. She'd cry, then she'd be fine.

S2.say: I'd say it's a big shock and the government should help sensibly with mortgages and training, not throw money at everything. I might even post once, which I never do.
S2.think: I think the plant would go fully automatic fast since it's halfway there, and my partner's reception job could go too. I'd be lying if I said I had a plan.
S2.do: Writes the household budget in the first month and sells the newer car to clear the loan. Looks straight away for local work robots aren't doing yet, and asks his partner's parents for mortgage help.
S2.quote: Asking him for money is like admitting I didn't.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario breaks Tomas's usual calm because both household jobs are exposed. He moves quickly to practical steps but admits there's no real plan. The story about his father-in-law shows how much pride is tied up in being the provider.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people start now. I'd say the company should tell us early and help us retrain. And I'd tell my friends not to wait until year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to change, and I think I'd do it once I saw others doing it. Maybe I'd train as an electrician or a maintenance tech, then I'm fixing machines for a few more years. But in the end, if robots do everything, maybe even that goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd watch what the early movers do. By year two, I'd start an evening course, probably electrical, because Mo's cousin did it and got a job at the wind farm. I'd save every bit of overtime and try to get to two months of savings by year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. It's a clear problem with a clear-ish answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch the early movers for a year. Does that cost you anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. The first people on the courses get the first jobs. But the first people also pick the wrong thing sometimes. I'd rather be second and right than first and wrong. That's just how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, it's survival. With five, I get a real change of job. Maybe not a forever job, but a few good years. And the kids get a dad who looks like he knows what he's doing, which matters.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough if people start now, and the company should tell us early and help retrain. I'd tell friends not to wait until year four.
S3.think: I think five years lets me change once I see others doing it, maybe to electrician or maintenance tech. But if robots do everything, even that may go in the end.
S3.do: Watches what early movers do in year one, then starts an evening electrical course in year two. Saves all overtime pay and aims for two months of savings by year three.
S3.feel: Anxious but steady, facing a clear problem with a clear-ish answer.
S3.quote: I'd rather be second and right than first and wrong.
S3.fieldNote: Tomas tells friends not to wait until year four while himself planning to wait a year, and when asked he owned the trade-off. His model for change is people he knows: Mo's cousin at the wind farm. He thinks about how he'll look to his kids, not just about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's plan it like grown-ups. Schools, training, help for older workers. I'd vote for whoever has the most sensible plan, not the loudest one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be fine for a while. I can change jobs, save a bit, maybe pay off more of the mortgage. The thing I can't plan for is the end, when it's all here. Nobody knows what that looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start the electrical course in two or three years, once I've seen it work for others. Pay a bit extra off the mortgage each year. And talk to Yusuf seriously about his future, because he'll be finishing school right in the middle of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about the kids. I'd be okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Yusuf to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn a trade with his hands and his head, like electrician or plumber, and to be good with the AI tools as well. He wants to be a footballer. I'd say, sure, and learn wiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years make you less of a second mover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd still wait to see. But with ten years, being second still leaves plenty of time. That's the nice thing about the slow one. Patience doesn't cost you much.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's plan it like grown-ups, with schools, training and help for older workers. I'd vote for the most sensible plan, not the loudest.
S4.think: I think I'd be fine for a while and could change jobs, save and pay more off the mortgage. What I can't plan for is the end, when nobody knows what life looks like.
S4.do: Starts the electrical course in two or three years once it's proven for others, and overpays the mortgage a little each year. Talks seriously with his son about a trade combined with AI skills.
S4.feel: Uneasy, mostly about his children's future.
S4.quote: He wants to be a footballer. I'd say, sure, and learn wiring.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years suits Tomas's temperament: being second costs little when there's time. His worry moves to his son, who'd leave school in the middle of the change. He wants sensible, not loud, politics.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Both Nadia and me at once, with nothing saved. What would help is something to hold the mortgage for a while, a pause or a cheap loan, so you have time to find the next thing without losing the house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about friends at work. If it comes down to me or Mo for one job, that's going to break something. Patience doesn't help with that.

headlineQuote: When we beat our record, I bring in pastries.
portrait: Tomas Ibrahim is a 43-year-old lead operator on a bottling line who tracks every bottle per minute in a notebook but has never written down the household budget. He uses AI now and then for shift reports and won't adopt anything until he's seen it work elsewhere. He's calm about the AI Plateau and uneasy about Steady Disruption, where his main fear is competing with his friend Mo. AGI in 2 years alarms him because his partner's reception job is exposed too, and he'd have to ask his father-in-law for help. With 5 or 10 years he plans an electrical course, taken a little after the early movers, and worries mostly about his son's future.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he and his partner could lose their jobs at once with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: Something to hold the mortgage for a while, like a pause or a cheap loan, so the family has time to find new work without losing the house.
